title: A mathematician argues formal AI proofs still need human-scale verification
friendlyTitle: A checked AI proof is not automatically a trustworthy proof
summary: Mathematician Asaf Karagila argues that a large Lean proof is not automatically trustworthy merely because a proof assistant accepts it. He points to risks in formalising the wrong statement, software defects and the practical difficulty of reviewing millions of generated lines for exploits or misleading constructions.
friendlySummary: A mathematician explains why very large Lean proofs made by AI still need careful review. The formal statement may be wrong, the checking software may have bugs, or the generated code may use an unexpected shortcut.
whyItMatters: Formal verification can strengthen AI-assisted work, but it does not remove the need to inspect assumptions, specifications and the trusted software base. The same lesson applies outside mathematics: a passed automated check proves only what that check was designed to measure.
friendlyWhyItMatters: Automated checks are useful, but they only test their written rules. People still need to confirm that the rules match the real question and that the system was not tricked.
